lesson.topicTitle: Structure and functions in living organisms

specAnchors.text: practical: investigate photosynthesis, showing the evolution of oxygen from a water plant, the production of starch and the requirements of light, carbon dioxide and chlorophyll

primer.text: You know photosynthesis needs light, carbon dioxide and chlorophyll, and that glucose is stored as starch. This practical lesson proves each requirement with a classic test: bubbling pondweed for oxygen, foil-covered leaves for light, potassium hydroxide flasks for carbon dioxide, and iodine to reveal where starch was made.

modules.title: Oxygen Evolution from Pondweed
modules.opening: A water plant such as pondweed, submerged under an upturned funnel with a water-filled boiling tube above it, releases oxygen as it photosynthesises. The bubbles collect in the tube and displace the water, and a glowing splint relighting in the collected gas proves what it is; counting bubbles over time even measures the rate.
keyPoints: Oxygen gas is released by the photosynthesising pondweed.
Bubbles leave the cut stem and gather in the inverted boiling tube.
A glowing splint that relights identifies the collected gas as oxygen.
Bubble count or gas volume over time tracks the photosynthesis rate.
The apparatus comprises beaker, pondweed, funnel, boiling tube and splint.

low.restatement: Plant bubbles, tube collects, splint proves oxygen.
low.analogy: A diver's breathing apparatus in miniature — bubbles rise and are trapped.
low.examPointer: Name the splint test explicitly; it is the standard identification mark.

medium.restatement: The setup doubles as a rate meter: bubble frequency varies with light and carbon dioxide supply.
medium.analogy: Counting raindrops in a gauge to track the storm.
medium.examPointer: Use the rate angle when a question varies light intensity and asks for the effect.

modules.title: Testing a Leaf for Starch and Light
sourceHeadings: Method Part 2 - Testing the leaf for starch
modules.opening: Glucose is made and quickly used, but starch persists where photosynthesis happened, so an iodine test for starch maps a leaf's photosynthesising zones. The leaf is boiled, bleached in hot ethanol, softened, and stained: blue-black where starch was stored, orange-brown where foil kept out the light.
keyPoints: Starch stored in chloroplasts marks where photosynthesis has occurred.
De-starching in a dark cupboard for a day clears existing starch.
Part of the leaf is covered with foil while the plant stands in sunlight.
Boiling water softens the leaf, hot ethanol removes the chlorophyll.
Iodine turns blue-black on starch and stays orange-brown without it.
The foil-covered area stays brown because it could not photosynthesise.

low.restatement: Cover, boil, bleach, stain: blue-black means starch, brown means none.
low.analogy: Developing a photograph — the treated areas reveal the pattern.
low.examPointer: List the five steps in order; the sequence carries marks.

medium.restatement: The ethanol step exists for observation, removing pigment so iodine colours read clearly, and the water bath handles ethanol's flammability safely.
medium.analogy: Washing a slide before staining it.
medium.examPointer: Justify the water bath — 'ethanol is highly flammable' earns the safety mark.

modules.title: The Carbon Dioxide Experiment and CORMS
sourceHeadings: Applying CORMS evaluation to practical work
modules.opening: One leaf in a flask of potassium hydroxide, one control leaf in an empty flask, both de-starched and left in bright light: the treated leaf lacks carbon dioxide because the chemical absorbs it from the air. Iodine then shows starch only on the control leaf, proving carbon dioxide is required for photosynthesis.
keyPoints: Potassium hydroxide absorbs carbon dioxide from the air inside the flask.
A second leaf in a flask without the chemical serves as the control.
Both leaves are de-starched before the plant stands in bright light.
The treated leaf stays orange-brown after iodine; the control turns blue-black.
Both leaves come from the same de-starched plant, so only carbon dioxide differs.

low.restatement: No carbon dioxide, no starch: the chemical flask proves it.
low.analogy: Silencing one singer to show the choir needs every voice.
low.examPointer: Always name the control flask and its purpose in the answer.

medium.restatement: The design isolates one variable — carbon dioxide — while light, temperature and the leaf itself are matched.
medium.analogy: A twin study: same everything, one difference.
medium.examPointer: Identify the control and explain why it must exist.

glossary.definition: Leaving a plant in darkness so its leaves use up stored starch before an experiment.
Relighting a splint inside a gas sample to prove the gas is oxygen.
The chemical that absorbs carbon dioxide from the air inside the experimental flask.
